defects.description: Creating a claim and starting its workflow, or recording a decision and delivering its callback, are separate writes without a durable dispatch record or reconciliation mechanism. A crash between these operations can strand a claim; deterministic execution names prevent some duplicates but do not repair missing dispatches.

The seven-year, per-step business audit is not sufficiently defined. Step Functions execution history expires, while CloudTrail resource-access records and mutable claim records do not establish a retained business-transition archive; execution-log contents and retention are also unspecified.

Specify an upload-finalization operation that verifies completed documents and binds their object versions before starting automated checks; the combined create/upload-URL/start handler leaves this sequencing ambiguous.
Make per-route customer-versus-adjuster authorization and claim-ownership checks explicit; separate user pools and valid JWTs alone do not describe these application permissions.
Document the email send/acknowledgment ambiguity: a notification-sent flag suppresses known repeats but cannot make SES acceptance and the DynamoDB update atomic.

reviews.summary: The service choices are appropriate, but crash-consistent workflow dispatch and a retained business audit need substantial strengthening.

defects.description: Specify actual document and audit retention durations, deletion policies, and the assumed regulatory baseline rather than leaving the retention clarification answered only by storage mechanisms.
Define the business disposition and customer-notification policy when the 14-day approval window expires; timeout handling is present, but its outcome is not stated.

reviews.summary: The design covers the workflow with durable dispatch, reconciliation, authorization, and archived business events, leaving mainly policy decisions to finalize.

defects.description: The subscriber-stream relay has no specified stream failure destination or reconciliation process. DynamoDB Streams retention is finite, so the downstream SQS queue protects only successfully enqueued jobs; the claim that the stream-based outbox avoids losing events is too strong.
Specify cache behaviors and keys that cache only public content, bypass authenticated and presigned-URL operations, and define acceptable post-update staleness.
Issuing a presigned URL is not an S3 object write by the API handler; show the author's direct HTTPS upload to S3 and distinguish URL signing from object access.

reviews.summary: The design meets the global, low-cost serverless blog requirements well, but the stream-to-email relay still needs durable failure recovery.

defects.description: No reader delivery path is defined for originals or thumbnails: CloudFront has only the static-site and API origins, and the photo bucket has neither a CloudFront origin nor another authorized download mechanism. Add a private media origin and corresponding cache behavior.

The thumbnail function writes into its triggering bucket without a specified input-prefix filter or separate output bucket. Generated thumbnails can retrigger processing, creating an invocation loop and uncontrolled cost.

The shared DLQ description does not distinguish asynchronous S3 invocation failures from DynamoDB Streams event-source-mapping failures. Streams require their own failure configuration, and an SQS on-failure destination contains invocation metadata rather than a durable copy of the original stream records, so replay after stream expiry is not established.

Authors and subscribers share a user pool, but no author-specific scopes, group checks, or application authorization are specified for post writes and upload authorization. A valid user-pool token alone does not distinguish an author from a subscriber.
Define public-read cache keys and TTLs, forward authorization where needed, and explicitly disable caching for authenticated or presigned-URL operations.

reviews.summary: The core services fit, but media delivery, author authorization, thumbnail loop prevention, and stream failure recovery are insufficiently specified.

defects.description: The checkout Lambda is placed in a private subnet but must write to DynamoDB, with no DynamoDB VPC endpoint or NAT/egress path provided. Only the SageMaker call mentions a VPC endpoint; as drawn, the required transaction-and-score persistence cannot complete.

The claimed VPC-only inference access is not established by placing the model in a private subnet. Specify the SageMaker Runtime interface endpoint and access policies that restrict invocation through it; model-container VPC connectivity and private access to the inference API are distinct configurations.

The design claims two-AZ checkout availability but attaches the scoring Lambda only to the AZ1 subnet. Configure the function with private subnets in both Availability Zones rather than relying on the endpoint's stated availability.

Using the transaction ID as a DynamoDB key does not by itself make checkout retries idempotent: an ordinary PutItem replaces the existing item. Specify conditional persistence, retry-payload validation, and returning the committed score so retries cannot overwrite an earlier result after a model change.
Add explicit candidate evaluation and a guarded endpoint rollout with rollback criteria before monthly retraining changes the payment-time model.

reviews.summary: SageMaker is the right hosting choice, but the depicted persistence network path is blocking and the HA, private-access, and idempotency claims need correction.

defects.description: Enable and define transaction-table recovery, such as DynamoDB point-in-time recovery, to protect persisted payment scores against accidental modification or deletion.
Specify the checkout latency budget, bounded inference timeouts and retries, and autoscaling minimum/maximum capacity and targets so scaling delays do not exhaust the synchronous request budget.
Extend the evaluation gate with an explicit production rollout and rollback policy for endpoint updates.

reviews.summary: The design directly satisfies managed real-time PyTorch serving and monthly retraining with sound persistence and access controls, needing modest recovery and rollout hardening.

preference.why: Its transactional outbox, scheduled reconciliation, explicit authorization, and durable business audit better satisfy resumability and per-step auditability.
It provides a complete cached media-delivery path, separates author authentication, and explicitly prevents thumbnail recursion while buffering asynchronous work.
It avoids the incomplete private-network topology, defines safe transaction retries and persistence-before-success, and provides evaluated monthly releases with trigger failure capture.
